stories.headline: Russian bombs hit a school used as an aid centre in southern Ukraine; dozens killed
stories.what_happened: On 2 November 2026 Russian aerial bombs hit a school used to hand out humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, a village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region. At least 40 people were reported killed and rescuers were still searching the rubble.
stories.why_it_matters: Aid points and shelters are meant to protect civilians, and Ukraine's president said the attack showed Russia does not want to calm the war.

key_facts.fact: The attack was on Monday 2 November 2026 in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, about 20 km from the front line.
The Kyiv Independent reported at least 33 killed, including two rescue workers and four police officers; the toll was later reported as 40.
Zelensky said Russia dropped nine more aerial bombs on a shelter where people had gone for safety after the first strike.
Zelensky said more than 30 people might still be under the rubble, and rescue efforts continued.
The settlement has been considered front-line since November 2025 amid repeated Russian guided aerial bomb attacks.
Zelensky called it an 'exceptionally horrific strike' and said Russian forces could not have been unaware that aid was distributed there weekly.
Russia's Defense Ministry said the strike targeted Ukraine's military and claimed as many as 25 Ukrainian service members were killed; Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians.
Zelensky said: 'Ukraine needs air defense support right now.'
Guided aerial bombs fitted with wing kits can travel tens of kilometres, letting aircraft strike from outside air defence range.

stories.headline: NASA's Swift space telescope is falling back to Earth after 22 years
stories.what_happened: NASA's Swift Observatory, launched in 2004 to watch gamma-ray bursts, was expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere on 4 November 2026. NASA expected most of it to burn up.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how satellites that cannot raise their own orbit slowly sink, and how agencies track them.

key_facts.fact: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory launched in 2004, was designed for a two-year primary mission and operated for nearly 22 years.
Swift's main target was gamma-ray bursts, using three telescopes and rapidly alerting other observatories.
The US Space Force estimated re-entry at about 3:30 a.m. EST on 4 November, with an uncertainty of eleven hours.
The spacecraft weighs roughly 3,200 pounds and NASA expects most of it to burn up, though some parts may survive.
Any surviving debris would fall between latitudes 20.6° N and 20.6° S; NASA estimated the injury risk to a person at about one in 2,100.
Increased solar activity expands the upper atmosphere and adds drag, and Swift has no thrusters and cannot raise its own altitude.
In August NASA and Katalyst Space said a LINK spacecraft would not capture or boost Swift because of an attitude control problem.

stories.headline: Democrats win control of the US Senate and House in the midterm elections
stories.what_happened: In elections on 3 November 2026 Democrats were projected to win both chambers of Congress, with the Senate at least 54 seats and the House more than 250. A few close races were still being counted.
stories.why_it_matters: Congress writes laws and controls spending, so Democratic control gives them power to block nominees, investigate, and shape laws for Trump's last two years.

key_facts.fact: CNBC's Election Desk projected Democrats would win at least 250 House seats and Republicans at least 160, as of early Wednesday.
CBS projected Democrats winning the House with an estimate of 251 to 268 seats; about 75 House races were undetermined in its early-morning update.
Democrats were on track for at least 54 Senate seats and Republicans at least 42; Alaska and Mississippi were uncalled midday Wednesday.
Fifty-one Senate seats are needed for control.
In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom led Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by under 100 votes with 96% counted.
Democrats' Senate flips included Texas (James Talarico over Ken Paxton), Ohio (Sherrod Brown over Jon Husted), Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, Maine and Michigan.
Democrats flipped five Republican-held governorships: Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada, giving them at least 28 governorships, their first majority since 2010.
Democratic House control gives the party subpoena and investigative power over Trump's final two years; Trump said he will use his veto power as needed.
Hakeem Jeffries is expected to become Speaker; Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek the minority leader post.
The Dow was up about 3% midday, its biggest one-day gain since April 2025.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu hits Andhra Pradesh coast; thousands move to shelters
stories.what_happened: Severe Cyclonic Storm Murasu crossed the south Andhra Pradesh coast near Ongole in Prakasam district in the early hours of Tuesday 3 November 2026. It uprooted trees, toppled electricity poles and flooded low-lying areas. Thousands of people were moved to shelters.
stories.why_it_matters: It was the second cyclone to hit the region in a week, so people, farms and relief teams had little time to recover.

key_facts.fact: The India Meteorological Department said Murasu crossed the coast near Ongole in Prakasam district at around 1 am on Tuesday.
Murasu formed from a low-pressure system over the Bay of Bengal, became a cyclonic storm on 1 November and a severe cyclonic storm on 2 November.
Winds reached 100-110 km/h, with gusts up to 120 km/h.
The IMD expected the storm to weaken into a deep depression by Tuesday night and to dissipate fully by 5 November.
More than 30,000 hectares of standing crops were damaged across 15 districts; Krishna, Bapatla and Nandyal were worst hit, and paddy, cotton and maize suffered most.
Salt pans were flooded, causing losses for farmers and workers.
10,805 people were moved to cyclone shelters, according to the Tribune report; the state set up 171 relief camps and distributed 14,810 food packets.

Prakhar Jain, managing director of the Andhra Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority, said no deaths or injuries had been reported at the time of the Tribune report; a later live blog said at least two people died in cyclone-related incidents.
NDRF deployed 14 teams in Andhra Pradesh, three of them moved from Tamil Nadu.
In Odisha, 1,65,809 people were evacuated from six southern districts.
The IMD advised fishermen not to go to sea until the morning of 4 November.
Home Minister Amit Shah said he had spoken to Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu and that NDRF and SDRF teams were already on the ground.
Murasu was the second cyclone to hit the region in a week, after Cyclone Arnab, which killed seven people in Andhra Pradesh according to a 29 October report.

stories.geography: Ongole, Prakasam district, Andhra Pradesh, on India's east coast on the Bay of Bengal; Odisha to the north-east

stories.headline: Trees have an inner sense of shape that helps them straighten
stories.what_happened: French researchers found that trees sense their own shape and grow special wood on either side of the trunk to pull it upright.
stories.why_it_matters: It could help foresters and farmers breed straighter trees and crops that stay standing.

key_facts.fact: The study, by INRAE researchers in France, was published in New Phytologist.
Young poplar trees were laid horizontally and their stems curved upward over time.
Tension wood on the upper side of the stem pulled the stem upward.
After about ten days the trees were moved onto a rotating platform inside a sphere lit evenly from all directions, which removed steady gravity and light cues.
In that setup, tension wood on the upper side stopped forming and identical tension wood formed on the opposite side, pulling the other way.
The opposing forces gradually straightened the stems over several weeks.
The researchers say trees use proprioception, an internal sense of their own shape, to decide where tension wood forms.
The authors suggest it could help trees recover from storms and landslides, and inform breeding for straighter trees and crops less prone to falling over before harvest.
Bruno Moulia, INRAE research director: 'What we have uncovered is a genuine sensorimotor loop operating in the woody parts of trees!'

stories.headline: Museum frogs reveal a fungus behind a 50-year-old mystery
stories.what_happened: Scientists tested preserved amphibians from Brazil's Atlantic Forest and found evidence that the chytrid fungus caused sharp declines in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows museum collections can solve old mysteries and help protect wildlife.

key_facts.fact: Researchers tested over 370 preserved amphibians from 17 species collected at the Boracéia Biological Station in Brazil's Atlantic Forest.
Amphibian populations there declined sharply between 1979 and 1982.
None of the specimens collected before 1979 tested positive for the chytrid fungus; more than half of those collected in the 1980s did.
The fungus is Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis; it is believed to have originated in Asia and spread worldwide in the 1970s and 1980s.
The most severely declined species showed no detectable infection in the specimens, while stable species often carried it.
The researchers' proposed explanation, which is a hypothesis, is that some species tolerate infection while very susceptible ones died so quickly that infected animals were rarely collected.
Between 2022 and 2024 the team made six visits and found 12 of the 17 historical species; most appear to have recovered, although the fungus is still present.
The findings were published in Molecular Ecology, and apply to Boracéia, not automatically to the rest of the Atlantic Forest.

sources.title: A 50-year-old Mystery of Vanishing Frogs Reveals a Hidden Killer

stories.headline: Ape fossil from Egypt could change the story of ape origins
stories.what_happened: A 17-18-million-year-old jaw found at Wadi Moghra in Egypt is the first definitive fossil ape from North Africa, and may change where scientists think living apes began.
stories.why_it_matters: It suggests the ancestors of living apes may have lived in North Africa and the Middle East rather than only East Africa.

key_facts.fact: The fossil species is Masripithecus moghraensis, about 17 to 18 million years old, from Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt.
It is the first definitive fossil ape found in North Africa.
The team from Mansoura University in Egypt and the University of Southern California found it on expeditions in 2023 and 2024; it was published in Science on 26 March 2026.
The authors' analyses point to North Africa and the Middle East as the likely home of the common ancestor of all living apes, challenging the East African origin model.
The jaw has large canines and rounded, textured chewing surfaces, suggesting a mainly fruit diet that could handle harder foods like nuts.
Only part of a lower jaw has been found, so its body size and behaviour are unknown.
The researchers do not claim it was a direct ancestor of humans or living apes.

sources.title: Ancient Ape Fossil in Egypt Could Rewrite the Story of Human Origins

stories.headline: Scientists watch virus-like particles build themselves one piece at a time
stories.what_happened: Oxford researchers used a technique that weighs single molecules to watch an engineered virus-like particle assemble, learning how it avoids mistakes.
stories.why_it_matters: Understanding assembly could help design antiviral drugs and vaccines.

key_facts.fact: The Oxford study was published in Nature.
The team studied an engineered virus-like particle made of 60 protein units.
They used mass photometry, a technique developed at Oxford that measures the mass of single molecules from the light they scatter.
Early protein connections are weak, so wrong combinations can separate and retry.
A closed ring of five larger building blocks is the first highly stable structure, and later stages need fewer extra blocks, so growth speeds up.
The earliest stage, nucleation, is the most difficult step.
Understanding this could support antiviral drugs that disrupt capsid assembly and improve vaccine design.
Dr Roi Asor: 'The weak interactions give the system room to make mistakes.'

sources.title: Oxford Scientists Discover How Viruses Build Themselves Without a Blueprint

stories.headline: UK prime minister opens door to an apology for the slave trade but rules out reparations
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his government will consider apologising for the first time for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade, but rejected reparations. He offered a 'structured dialogue' with affected nations ahead of the Commonwealth leaders' meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.
stories.why_it_matters: A formal apology from the British state would be a major step in how the country talks about its history, and Caribbean leaders say reparations remain an open question.

key_facts.fact: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his government will consider apologising for the first time for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade, but he rejects reparations.
He wrote in the Guardian on Saturday that Britain must acknowledge its 'complicated history' to protect the Commonwealth.
He offered a 'structured dialogue' with affected nations and said he will hear calls for a formal state apology.
He said people living today cannot be held liable for historical wrongs they did not personally commit.
He said Britain 'participated in the trade in human lives' and expressed sorrow for the suffering it caused.

Instead of reparations he wants to address debt: working with wealthy nations and investors to give vulnerable countries longer repayment periods and lower interest rates; former PM Gordon Brown will attend the Commonwealth meeting to support this.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley welcomed Burnham's acknowledgment and openness to an apology but said differences remain on reparations.
Antigua and Barbuda Prime Minister Gaston Browne called the comments a 'significant and welcome development' and said the Caribbean's position on reparatory justice is unchanged.
Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and outlawed slavery across the British Empire in 1833; the trade involved the transfer of several million people from Africa.

King Charles III, on a nine-day Caribbean trip, said in Nassau in the Bahamas that he acknowledged 'the great suffering and injustices of the past' but did not apologise, because the monarch speaks on behalf of the elected government.

numbers.label: Slavery outlawed across the British Empire

stories.why_it_matters: Countries joining the EU would change borders, trade and who has a say in Europe.

key_facts.fact: The Euronews EU Enlargement Summit took place in Brussels on 3 November 2026, with leaders from Ukraine, Albania, Moldova, Georgia, North Macedonia, Armenia, Croatia and the European Council.
European Council President António Costa called enlargement 'the best geopolitical investment Europe has made' and said he has visited all candidate countries several times.
Costa said the fourth EU-Western Balkans Summit would be held in three weeks.
Ukraine has made formal progress since the change of government in Hungary and is still expected to open all negotiating clusters before the end of 2026.

Montenegro is closest to the finish line but is stalled by bilateral issues with Croatia rooted in the Yugoslav Wars; its EU minister said negotiating chapters could close this year, with accession following in 2028.
Albania is considered the second-closest candidate.
Moldova is progressing so quickly that the Commission has reallocated internal resources to keep pace.
Georgia's accession has effectively halted amid democratic backsliding; Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said it is 'a candidate country only on paper'.
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković warned that France's upcoming presidential elections could derail the accession process.

stories.headline: European Commission publishes guidelines to help families prepare for emergencies
stories.what_happened: On 4 November, Commissioner Hadja Lahbib presented non-binding Population Preparedness Guidelines at the European Civil Protection Forum, including advice to be able to cope for 72 hours in an emergency.
stories.why_it_matters: Floods, storms and other crises can cut power or water; being ready for the first three days helps people stay safe.

key_facts.fact: Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management Hadja Lahbib presented the measures at the European Civil Protection Forum.
The non-binding Population Preparedness Guidelines help people meet essential needs during the first 72 hours of an emergency, using emergency supplies and grab bags.
The guidelines propose adding preparedness to early childhood and primary curricula, with teacher training, and keeping lessons free of fear or anxiety.
They also cover making preparedness accessible to people with disabilities and giving citizens timely, accessible and reliable information before, during and after emergencies.
The Commission proposes an annual EU Preparedness Day on 23 October, starting in 2027, marking the creation of the Civil Protection Mechanism in 2001, now 25 years old.
The European Citizens' Panel on Preparedness had 150 citizens, met from March to May 2026 and recommended an annual EU Preparedness Week.

stories.headline: Russia strikes a school used as shelter in southeastern Ukraine, Zelensky says
stories.what_happened: CNN reported on 3 November that Russia dropped at least nine bombs on a school building in southeastern Ukraine where people had taken shelter, and Zelensky called it one of the war's deadliest attacks. It came before another large barrage of drones and missiles aimed at energy infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on power networks and civilian buildings affect millions of people as winter approaches.

key_facts.fact: Russia dropped at least nine bombs on a school building in southeastern Ukraine where people had taken shelter, and Zelensky called it one of the deadliest attacks of the war.

Zelensky said the attack came just before Russia launched a barrage of hundreds of drones and dozens of missiles aimed at Ukraine's energy infrastructure, despite Trump's calls for an energy ceasefire.
Ukraine's air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since Saturday evening.
Russian strikes hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.

sources.title: Russian bombing of Ukrainian aid center is one of the war's 'deadliest attacks,' Zelensky says
Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine, despite Trump's energy ceasefire push

stories.headline: Europe weighs releasing emergency diesel stocks as US pressure grows
stories.what_happened: Earlier this autumn the Trump administration asked EU governments to release 120 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves over 180 days, and floated a US diesel export ban. EU governments held emergency talks.
stories.why_it_matters: Diesel moves goods and powers farms and lorries, so prices affect shop prices.

key_facts.fact: The Trump administration reportedly asked EU governments to release 120 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves over 180 days.
Washington floated a US diesel export ban to lower domestic prices before the 3 November midterms.
The US supplied half of the EU's diesel imports in August, according to the European Commission.
A French proposal would have European countries release 50 million barrels, with IEA members also contributing.
The Commission said supplies were stable for the time being, and reserves are also needed as insurance because the Iran war has disrupted Gulf supply.

stories.geography: European Union; United States; Persian Gulf

sources.title: Trump vs Europe as US presses for release of emergency diesel stocks

stories.headline: EU and UK to hold second summit in Brussels on 20 November
stories.what_happened: António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen will welcome Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Brussels on 20 November for the second EU-UK summit.
stories.why_it_matters: The summit will review how the UK and EU work together on defence, energy, trade and migration.

key_facts.fact: The second EU-UK summit takes place in Brussels on 20 November; leaders will review progress since the 2025 London summit, covering defence and security, energy, agrifood rules, climate, people-to-people contacts, and migration and law enforcement.
A joint declaration is expected at the end of the summit.
An EU-Western Balkans summit follows in Brussels on 25 November.

sources.title: EU-UK summit to take place in Brussels on 20 November
